hook.text: 93% of drivers say they're above average. Half of them, by definition, are wrong. And they'd bet money on it.

buildup.text: Overconfidence bias means people's certainty in their judgments exceeds their actual accuracy.

discovery.text: When people say they're 90% certain, they're right only about 70% of the time. The gap is consistent.

twist.text: Experts are often more overconfident than novices—expertise breeds certainty faster than it breeds accuracy.

climax.text: Overconfidence fuels bubbles, failed projects, and wars. It's the most damaging bias of all.

details.summary: People consistently overestimate the accuracy of their knowledge and predictions. When they say they are 90 percent confident, they are typically correct only about 70 percent of the time.
details.whyItMatters: Overconfidence leads to inadequate preparation, excessive risk, and poor planning. It is a leading cause of project overruns, business failures, and financial losses.
takeaways: Subjective confidence consistently exceeds actual accuracy
Experts are often just as overconfident as non-experts
It is among the most robust findings in judgment research

faq.question: Are there fields where people are well calibrated?
faq.answer: Weather forecasters and professional poker players tend to be well calibrated because they receive frequent, clear feedback on their predictions. Most domains lack this immediate feedback loop, so overconfidence persists unchecked. Calibration training can help in any field.

faq.question: How can you reduce your own overconfidence?
faq.answer: Consider the opposite of your belief. Assign confidence intervals wider than feels comfortable. Track your predictions and compare them to outcomes. Seek feedback from people who disagree with you. These practices improve calibration over time.
